As of 330 AM Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... In an active pattern with daily threats of severe 
wind and flooding for the next few days, there is now a Slight risk 
(Level 2 of 5) of both severe thunderstorms with damaging wet 
downbursts and excessive rain/flash flooding across cntl NC today.

An upr wave/shortwave trough, evident in GOES-E water vapor data 
from the Virginias to middle TN this morning, and which has 
amplified from the upr MS Valley and upr Great Lakes since Sun 
morning, will pivot slowly across and offshore the srn Middle 
Atlantic, Carolinas, and GA through early tonight. It will be 
preceded by MCVs, apparent in regional radar data over the NC 
Sandhills and srn Coastal Plain this morning and others likely to 
form from subsequent convective clusters over cntl and ern NC later 
today into early tonight. 

In the lwr-levels and at the surface, regional VWP and surface 
observational data depict a trough and associated frontal zone in 
the 925 mb to surface layer roughly along the NC/VA border this 
morning. This boundary, and post-frontal stratus, will likely 
continue to settle swd and into the nrn Piedmont and nrn Coastal 
Plain of NC this morning. It will be preceded by at least a couple 
of aggregate outflow boundaries evident in recent and earlier 
regional radar and surface observational data from cntl SC through 
ern NC and also over the NC Sandhills and srn/wrn Piedmont. 

The surface-925 mb front, one that should be strengthened through 
differential diabatic heating along related low stratus after 
daybreak, will probably serve as a primary focus for renewed deep 
convective development with diurnal heating of an unseasonably 
moist/humid airmass from late morning through this evening. However, 
other cells may develop and cluster along the aforementioned outflow 
boundaries and also along a possible separate differential heating 
zone from mid-level cloud debris from the aforementioned MCV. All 
will occur in a deeply moist environment characterized by PWs of 
around 2" (slightly below 2" at GSO in recent RAOBs and slightly 
above 2" at MHX), and amid ~10-20 kts of swly cloud layer and 850 mb 
flow, supportive of small upwind propagation/Corfidi vectors and 
related slow-moving/backbuilding multi-cell clusters along the 
myriad of surface boundaries in place. Scattered instances of flash 
flooding may result, as may damaging, wet downbursts. 

While forecast heat index values will probably at least briefly 
reach the 100-105 F range from the srn Piedmont to the Sandhills and 
srn and cntl Coastal Plain, the MCV and associated mid-level cloud 
canopy may linger well into the morning; and uncertainties exist 
with how much and quickly the environment will heat before 
additional convection likely develops along the features noted 
above. As such, forecast confidence is low in heat indices 
meeting/exceeding 105 F; and no additional Heat Advisories are 
planned at this time for today. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...  Continued periods of unsettled weather this week 
as a stalled front lingers across NC.

Broad and weak troughing over the eastern CONUS today will become 
reinforced by a more vigorous shortwave trough pivoting across the 
Great Lakes and southern Quebec on Tues. A low-amplitude likely 
convectively altered perturbation rippling through the basal portion 
of the trough is forecast to shift across the Ohio Valley Tues 
morning before potentially shifting across the southern Mid-Atlantic 
during peak heating. There are some notable timing differences with 
the low-predicitability feature, but nevertheless, enhanced westerly 
winds of > 30 kts are forecast to sink south and into North Carolina 
and overlap a continued moist and unstable environment. Although 
flow throughout the troposphere is not particularly strong, 
consistently veering winds with height will support curved 
hodographs capable of producing transient supercells and bowing 
segments. Any right-moving storm will have a storm motion of 
southeast and increase the likelihood that storms may drift into our 
region from VA. All hazards will be on the table for Tuesday, 
although damaging straight-line winds will be the most likely 
primary and more widespread hazard.

An upstream shortwave trough is forecast to cross the mountains 
Wednesday with an attendant surface cold front in tow. With PW's 
still at or near 2" and nearly 2000 J/KG of MLCAPE available, strong 
to severe storms are more than plausible with the front. 
Significantly lower PW's will follow the front with substantially 
lower precip chances Thursday through Saturday, although model 
inconsistencies regarding how far south the front and drier air push 
south results in an lower forecast confidence in a dry spell; 
especially with such a weak and progressive surface high and 
climatologically approaching the window when it is difficult for 
fronts to progress all the way through the Carolinas.
